3.1.4 BACTERIAL GROWTH In higher organisms growth refers to an increase in size and volume of organism but in bacteria growth refers to an increase in number. The growth of Bacteria takes place by binary fission. Binary fission is a form of asexual reproduction in single celled organisms by which one cell divide into two cells of the same size. A bacterial population grows in a geometric or exponential manner, with each generation producing 2 cells, 4 cells, 8 cells, 16 cells, 32 cells, 64 cells and so on. Bacteria need certain conditions to grow, and these conditions are not the same for all bacteria. Factors such as oxygen, pH, temperature and light affect the growth of microorganisms. Osmotic pressure, atmospheric pressure, and available moisture are some other additional factors that affect the growth of bacteria. The growth rate is also influenced by the composition of the growth medium. When the nutritive culture medium is inoculated with a given number of bacteria and incubated for a sufficient period, it gives a characteristic growth pattern of bacteria. The graphical representation of the number of living bacteria cells in a population over a period of time is called bacterial growth curve. The growth curve has four phases:
1. Lag phase

3. Stationary phase
The growth of bacteria reaches a state during which there is no net increase in bacterial
population as the number of dividing cells is equal to the number of dying cells and this phase
is called as stationary phase. This is due to depletion of nutrition and accumulation of toxic
wastes products as a byproduct in log phase.
4. Decline phase (Death phase)
As the nutrition decreases and accumulation of toxic waste product increases, the number of
dying cells begins to exceed the number of newly born cell during this phase.

3.1.5 CYANOBACTERIA Cyanobacteria or blue-green algae are a group of photosynthetic bacteria widely distributed in various aquatic habitats (fresh water and marine) and terrestrial habitat (moist soil). They may live singly or in colonies. They are one of the oldest life forms on earth. The red colour of red Biology, Grade 11 | 175

sea is due to the abundance of the planktonic cyanobacteria. Most of the Cyanobacteria contain the green pigment chlorophyll (also some other pigments), which helps retain energy from the sun and allows these organisms to pursue an autotrophic mode of nutrition. Some cyanobacteria live in symbiotic association with other organisms. They may be unicellular or multicellular. The multicellular forms are filamentous or colonial. Each cell is surrounded by a rigid cell wall which covered by mucilaginous sheath. The cell wall is followed by a plasma membrane made up of lipid and proteins. The cell lacks membrane -bound structures like mitochondria, Golgi bodies, chloroplast, etc. The photosynthetic pigments present in cell are chlorophyll a, carotene, xanthophyll and phycobillins and are present in chromatophore restricted to peripheral region of cytoplasm. At the centre of the cell there is presence of nucleoid that consists of DNA, RNA and protein. DNA is circular without histone protein. Flagella are absent. The filamentous chain of cyanobacteria covered by a slimy sheath is called trichome. Some filamentous cyanobacteria (e.g. Nostoc, Anabaena, Scytonema) possess special types of cells in filaments called heterocysts that are the site of nitrogen fixation. Cell division takes place by amitosis and mitosis. The reproduction takes place by vegetative and asexual methods. Sexual reproduction is completely absent.
